claim: Macaque caudal intraparietal (CIP) area neurons possess robust 3D visual representations.
source: We previously showed that macaque caudal intraparietal (CIP) area neurons possess robust 3D visual representations, carry choice- and saccade-related activity, and exhibit experience-dependent sensorimotor associations (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b, which is a previous study by the authors.

claim: Macaque CIP area neurons carry choice-related activity.
source: We previously showed that macaque caudal intraparietal (CIP) area neurons possess robust 3D visual representations, carry choice- and saccade-related activity, and exhibit experience-dependent sensorimotor associations (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Macaque CIP area neurons carry saccade-related activity.
source: We previously showed that macaque caudal intraparietal (CIP) area neurons possess robust 3D visual representations, carry choice- and saccade-related activity, and exhibit experience-dependent sensorimotor associations (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Macaque CIP area neurons exhibit experience-dependent sensorimotor associations.
source: We previously showed that macaque caudal intraparietal (CIP) area neurons possess robust 3D visual representations, carry choice- and saccade-related activity, and exhibit experience-dependent sensorimotor associations (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Higher-level 3D representations were more prevalent in CIP than V3A.
source: Higher-level 3D representations and choice-related activity were more prevalent in CIP than V3A.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript comparing V3A and CIP neurons.

claim: Choice-related activity was more prevalent in CIP than V3A.
source: Higher-level 3D representations and choice-related activity were more prevalent in CIP than V3A.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript comparing V3A and CIP neurons.

claim: Both V3A and CIP contained saccade-related activity that predicted the direction and timing of eye movements.
source: Both areas contained saccade-related activity that predicted the direction/timing of eye movements.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript analyzing saccade-related activity in both areas.

claim: The time course of saccade-related activity in CIP aligned with the temporally integrated V3A output.
source: Intriguingly, the time course of saccade-related activity in CIP aligned with the temporally integrated V3A output.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis comparing temporal dynamics of saccade-related activity between V3A and CIP.

claim: Sensorimotor associations between 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences were stronger in CIP than V3A.
source: Sensorimotor associations between 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences were stronger in CIP than V3A, and moderated by choice signals in both areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing sensorimotor associations between the two areas.

claim: Sensorimotor associations were moderated by choice signals in both V3A and CIP.
source: Sensorimotor associations between 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences were stronger in CIP than V3A, and moderated by choice signals in both areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing interaction effects between choice signals and sensorimotor associations.

claim: 3D spatial reasoning is a key predictor of engineering problem-solving ability.
source: For instance, 3D spatial reasoning is a key predictor of engineering problem-solving ability (Hsi et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hsi et al., 1997.

claim: High-level visual transformations occur in brain areas located at the parieto-occipital junction.
source: In particular, high-level visual transformations are thought to occur in brain areas located at the parieto-occipital junction (Tsao et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2003 and Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Parietal cortex implements sensorimotor transformations that map sensory representations to motor responses.
source: Parietal cortex is thought to then implement sensorimotor transformations that map those sensory representations to motor responses (Pause and Freund, 1989; Rushworth et al., 1997; Buneo and Andersen, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pause and Freund, 1989; Rushworth et al., 1997; Buneo and Andersen, 2006.

claim: Area CIP is a site of 3D visual processing.
source: Area CIP is a site of 3D visual processing (Taira et al., 2000; Tsutsui et al., 2002; Rosenberg et al., 2013; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014a; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014b), which is functionally correlated (Tsutsui et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019) and causally linked (Tsutsui et al., 2001; Van Dromme et al., 2016) to 3D perception.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: CIP 3D visual processing is functionally correlated to 3D perception.
source: Area CIP is a site of 3D visual processing (Taira et al., 2000; Tsutsui et al., 2002; Rosenberg et al., 2013; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014a; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014b), which is functionally correlated (Tsutsui et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019) and causally linked (Tsutsui et al., 2001; Van Dromme et al., 2016) to 3D perception.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tsutsui et al., 2003 and Elmore et al., 2019.

claim: CIP 3D visual processing is causally linked to 3D perception.
source: Area CIP is a site of 3D visual processing (Taira et al., 2000; Tsutsui et al., 2002; Rosenberg et al., 2013; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014a; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014b), which is functionally correlated (Tsutsui et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019) and causally linked (Tsutsui et al., 2001; Van Dromme et al., 2016) to 3D perception.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tsutsui et al., 2001 and Van Dromme et al., 2016.

claim: Saccade-related activity and sensorimotor associations in CIP may support goal-directed behaviors via connections to oculomotor and prehensile areas.
source: Saccade-related activity and sensorimotor associations in CIP may further support goal-directed behaviors (Chang et al., 2020b) via connections to oculomotor and prehensile areas (Lewis and Van Essen, 2000; Premereur et al., 2015; Van Dromme et al., 2016; Lanzilotto et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to anatomical connectivity studies and a previous functional study.

claim: Some V3A findings imply relatively low-level image processing such as spatiotemporal filtering.
source: Some imply relatively low-level image processing such as spatiotemporal filtering (Gaska et al., 1987; Gaska et al., 1988), basic stereoscopic depth selectivity (Anzai et al., 2011), and 2D direction selectivity (Nakhla et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gaska et al., 1987 and Gaska et al., 1988.

claim: Some V3A findings imply basic stereoscopic depth selectivity.
source: Some imply relatively low-level image processing such as spatiotemporal filtering (Gaska et al., 1987; Gaska et al., 1988), basic stereoscopic depth selectivity (Anzai et al., 2011), and 2D direction selectivity (Nakhla et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Anzai et al., 2011.

claim: Some V3A findings imply 2D direction selectivity.
source: Some imply relatively low-level image processing such as spatiotemporal filtering (Gaska et al., 1987; Gaska et al., 1988), basic stereoscopic depth selectivity (Anzai et al., 2011), and 2D direction selectivity (Nakhla et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nakhla et al., 2021.

claim: Other V3A findings link V3A to high-level processes underlying stable, allocentric representations of the world.
source: Other findings link V3A to high-level processes underlying stable, allocentric representations of the world. This includes combining visual and extraretinal signals to represent objects in non-retinal coordinates (Galletti and Battaglini, 1989; Galletti et al., 1990; Sauvan and Peterhans, 1999; Nakamura and Colby, 2002), distinguishing veridical object motion from self-induced retinal image motion (Galletti et al., 1990), and 3D spatial processing (Tsao et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: V3A combines visual and extraretinal signals to represent objects in non-retinal coordinates.
source: This includes combining visual and extraretinal signals to represent objects in non-retinal coordinates (Galletti and Battaglini, 1989; Galletti et al., 1990; Sauvan and Peterhans, 1999; Nakamura and Colby, 2002), distinguishing veridical object motion from self-induced retinal image motion (Galletti et al., 1990), and 3D spatial processing (Tsao et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galletti and Battaglini, 1989; Galletti et al., 1990; Sauvan and Peterhans, 1999; Nakamura and Colby, 2002.

claim: V3A distinguishes veridical object motion from self-induced retinal image motion.
source: This includes combining visual and extraretinal signals to represent objects in non-retinal coordinates (Galletti and Battaglini, 1989; Galletti et al., 1990; Sauvan and Peterhans, 1999; Nakamura and Colby, 2002), distinguishing veridical object motion from self-induced retinal image motion (Galletti et al., 1990), and 3D spatial processing (Tsao et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Galletti et al., 1990.

claim: V3A is involved in 3D spatial processing.
source: This includes combining visual and extraretinal signals to represent objects in non-retinal coordinates (Galletti and Battaglini, 1989; Galletti et al., 1990; Sauvan and Peterhans, 1999; Nakamura and Colby, 2002), distinguishing veridical object motion from self-induced retinal image motion (Galletti et al., 1990), and 3D spatial processing (Tsao et al., 2003; Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2003 and Elmore et al., 2019.

claim: V3A activity is modulated by attention and memory-related factors.
source: Furthermore, V3A activity is modulated by attention and memory-related factors, and some neurons show postsaccadic activity (Nakamura and Colby, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nakamura and Colby, 2000.

claim: Some V3A neurons show postsaccadic activity.
source: Furthermore, V3A activity is modulated by attention and memory-related factors, and some neurons show postsaccadic activity (Nakamura and Colby, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nakamura and Colby, 2000.

claim: The median visual response latency was shorter in V3A (46 ms) than CIP (52 ms).
source: Supporting a V3A-to-CIP hierarchy, the median visual response latency was shorter in V3A (46 ms) than CIP (52 ms) and the receptive fields were smaller in V3A than CIP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The receptive fields were smaller in V3A than CIP.
source: Supporting a V3A-to-CIP hierarchy, the median visual response latency was shorter in V3A (46 ms) than CIP (52 ms) and the receptive fields were smaller in V3A than CIP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 692 V3A neurons were recorded (Monkey L: N = 311; Monkey F: N = 263; Monkey W: N = 118).
source: To investigate the contributions of areas V3A and CIP to the transformation of retinal images into object-level representations and goal-directed sensorimotor processing, we compared the 3D selectivity, saccade-related properties, and sensorimotor associations of 692 V3A neurons (Monkey L: N = 311; Monkey F: N = 263; Monkey W: N = 118) and 437 previously analyzed CIP neurons (Monkey L: N = 218; Monkey F: N = 219) (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the sample size in the study.

claim: 437 CIP neurons were previously analyzed (Monkey L: N = 218; Monkey F: N = 219).
source: To investigate the contributions of areas V3A and CIP to the transformation of retinal images into object-level representations and goal-directed sensorimotor processing, we compared the 3D selectivity, saccade-related properties, and sensorimotor associations of 692 V3A neurons (Monkey L: N = 311; Monkey F: N = 263; Monkey W: N = 118) and 437 previously analyzed CIP neurons (Monkey L: N = 218; Monkey F: N = 219) (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the sample size from a previous study.

claim: For a 3D pose selective neuron, the shape of its 3D orientation tuning curve will be tolerant to distance, but its overall response amplitude (gain) should be distance-dependent.
source: For a 3D pose selective neuron, the shape of its 3D orientation tuning curve will be tolerant to distance, but its overall response amplitude (gain) should be distance-dependent (Janssen et al., 2000; Nguyenkim and DeAngelis, 2003; Alizadeh et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing this property of 3D pose selective neurons.

claim: A neuron selective for lower-level visual features (e.g., binocular disparity) will have 3D orientation tuning curves whose shape and gain are highly distance-dependent.
source: In contrast, a neuron selective for lower-level visual features (e.g., binocular disparity) will have 3D orientation tuning curves whose shape and gain are highly distance-dependent.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established principles of visual processing and contrast with 3D pose selective neurons.

claim: V3A contains a heterogeneous population of neurons whose functional properties range from processing low-level visual features to 3D object pose.
source: These examples suggest that V3A contains a heterogeneous population of neurons whose functional properties range from processing low-level visual features to 3D object pose.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from example neurons and population analyses showing variability in tolerance values.

claim: More neurons had 3D orientation tuning at 57 cm (fixation distance) than at the other distances in both V3A and CIP.
source: In both areas, more neurons had 3D orientation tuning at 57 cm (fixation distance) than at the other distances (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: CIP neurons were typically tuned for 3D orientation at more distances than V3A neurons.
source: However, CIP neurons were typically tuned for 3D orientation at more distances than V3A neurons (chi-squared test, across animals: χ2 = 21.2, p=2.9 × 10–4; Monkey L: χ2 = 13.0, p=0.01; Monkey F: χ2 = 8.7, p=0.07), implying greater convergence of orientation information across distance within CIP than V3A (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Both V3A and CIP represented the full span of 3D orientations at each distance.
source: In both V3A and CIP, the full span of 3D orientations was represented at each distance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that both areas can support neural codes for 3D pose.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: V3A neurons (median λ2 = 0.80) were more narrowly tuned than CIP neurons (median λ2 = 0.65).
source: First, there was a slight but significant tendency for V3A neurons (median λ2 = 0.80) to be more narrowly tuned than CIP neurons (median λ2 = 0.65; linear mixed-effects model with area, absolute distance from fixation, and animal as fixed effects, and neuron as a random effect, p=1.5 × 10–3; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The V3A tuning curves were less isotropic (more elongated; median λ1 = –1.62) than the CIP tuning curves (median λ1 = –0.92).
source: Second, the V3A tuning curves were less isotropic (more elongated; median λ1 = –1.62) than the CIP tuning curves (median λ1 = – 0.92), and the difference was significant (p=1.3 × 10–9; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The distributions of Φ peaked at approximately 90° in both V3A (median Φ = 88°) and CIP (median Φ = 89°), indicating that any anisotropy in the tuning curves generally occurred along the tilt/slant axes.
source: Lastly, the distributions of Φ peaked at approximately 90° in both V3A (median Φ = 88°) and CIP (median Φ = 89°), indicating that any anisotropy in the tuning curves generally occurred along the tilt/slant axes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A previous study found that 3D orientation was better discriminated based on the responses of individual V3A than CIP neurons.
source: A previous study found that 3D orientation was better discriminated based on the responses of individual V3A than CIP neurons (Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elmore et al., 2019.

claim: 3D orientation was most discriminable at the fixation distance in both V3A and CIP.
source: In both areas, the mean SODI had an inverted U-shape as a function of distance that peaked at 57 cm (fixation distance; Figure 3G). This indicates that 3D orientation was most discriminable at the fixation distance, which may be a downstream consequence of V1 neurons tending to prefer smaller binocular disparities (Prince et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3G and inference from V1 properties.

claim: SODI values across animals were significantly larger in V3A than CIP at the fixation distance.
source: Consistent with the Elmore et al., 2019 study, which measured 3D orientation tuning at the fixation distance only, we found that the SODI values across animals were significantly larger in V3A than CIP at the fixation distance (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test, p=1.1 × 10–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In V3A, the mean tolerance was 0.57 ± 6.7 × 10–3 SEM across animals (N = 692).
source: In V3A, the mean tolerance was 0.57 ± 6.7 × 10–3 SEM across animals (Figure 4A, orange bars; N = 692).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the measured tolerance values.

claim: In CIP, the mean tolerance was 0.66 ± 7.7 × 10–3 SEM across animals (N = 437).
source: In CIP, the mean tolerance was 0.66 ± 7.7 × 10–3 SEM across animals (Figure 4A, blue bars; N = 437).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the measured tolerance values.

claim: The tolerance values in CIP were significantly larger than in V3A.
source: As predicted, the tolerance values in CIP were significantly larger than in V3A (two-sample t-test, across animals: p=7.4 × 10–19; Monkey L: p=4.7 × 10–11; Monkey F: p=3.7 × 10–7), indicating that the shape of 3D orientation tuning curves was more similar across distance in CIP than V3A.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The angular deviations between preferred orientation at each distance and the principal orientation were significantly greater in V3A than CIP.
source: Across neurons, we then computed cumulative density functions over the angular deviations (Figure 4B) and found that the deviations were significantly greater in V3A than CIP (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, across animals: p=1.2 × 10–9; Monkey L: p=5.1 × 10–6; Monkey F: p=5.9 × 10–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: A transformation from lower-level visual features to higher-level 3D object representations occurs between V3A and CIP.
source: These analyses together suggest that a transformation from lower-level visual features to higher-level 3D object representations occurs between V3A and CIP.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the tolerance and angular deviation analyses.

claim: Behavioral tilt sensitivity increases as a function of slant.
source: We previously found that behavioral tilt sensitivity, which increases as a function of slant and has an inverted U-shape pattern as a function of distance from fixation (Chang et al., 2020a; Figure 2C and black curves in Figure 5), is correlated with neuronal tilt discriminability in CIP (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020a and data presented in Figure 2C and Figure 5.

claim: Behavioral tilt sensitivity has an inverted U-shape pattern as a function of distance from fixation.
source: We previously found that behavioral tilt sensitivity, which increases as a function of slant and has an inverted U-shape pattern as a function of distance from fixation (Chang et al., 2020a; Figure 2C and black curves in Figure 5), is correlated with neuronal tilt discriminability in CIP (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020a and data presented in Figure 2C and Figure 5.

claim: Behavioral tilt sensitivity is correlated with neuronal tilt discriminability in CIP.
source: We previously found that behavioral tilt sensitivity, which increases as a function of slant and has an inverted U-shape pattern as a function of distance from fixation (Chang et al., 2020a; Figure 2C and black curves in Figure 5), is correlated with neuronal tilt discriminability in CIP (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: The behavioral tilt sensitivities and TDI values were highly correlated across all 16 slant–distance combinations in V3A.
source: Indeed, the behavioral tilt sensitivities and TDI values were highly correlated across all 16 slant–distance combinations (Monkey L: Spearman r = 0.92, p=2.2 × 10–308; Monkey F: r = 0.98, p=2.2 × 10–308; Monkey W: r = 0.74, p=1.5 × 10–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation between behavioral and neuronal data.

claim: Neuronal tilt discriminability in both V3A and CIP was functionally correlated with the 3D tilt sensitivities of the monkeys across a wide range of viewing conditions.
source: Thus, neuronal tilt discriminability in both V3A and CIP was functionally correlated with the 3D tilt sensitivities of the monkeys across a wide range of viewing conditions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation analyses for both areas.

claim: Roughly half of CIP neurons carried choice-related activity during 3D orientation discrimination tasks.
source: Previous studies found that roughly half of CIP neurons carried choice-related activity during 3D orientation discrimination tasks (Elmore et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elmore et al., 2019 and Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: One study reported that choice-related activity was essentially non-existent in V3A, but only tested 23 neurons.
source: In contrast, one of those studies also reported that choice-related activity was essentially non-existent in V3A, but only tested 23 neurons (Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elmore et al., 2019.

claim: Choice-related activity is preferentially carried by CIP neurons with robust 3D pose tuning.
source: Given that choice-related activity is preferentially carried by CIP neurons with robust 3D pose tuning (Chang et al., 2020b), the dearth of V3A choice-related activity in the Elmore study could have occurred if the small sample mostly included neurons with low-level feature selectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: The onset of choice-related activity in V3A was 191 ms.
source: The onset of choice-related activity was defined as the first time point that the eight time courses significantly diverged (191 ms; ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of population time courses.

claim: The onset of choice-related activity in CIP was 202 ms.
source: In contrast, the onset of choice-related activity in CIP was 202 ms (see Figure 5A in Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Choice-related activity appeared first in V3A, which may reflect that choice signals in CIP contain a large bottom-up contribution from V3A.
source: The finding that choice-related activity appeared first in V3A may reflect that choice signals in CIP contain a large bottom-up contribution from V3A.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on the temporal ordering of choice-related activity.

claim: 172 (25%) V3A neurons carried significant choice-related activity.
source: Across the populations, 172 (25%) V3A and 201 (46%) CIP neurons carried significant choice-related activity (ANOVA, p<0.05; Figure 6B, inset bar plot).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the data.

claim: 201 (46%) CIP neurons carried significant choice-related activity.
source: Across the populations, 172 (25%) V3A and 201 (46%) CIP neurons carried significant choice-related activity (ANOVA, p<0.05; Figure 6B, inset bar plot).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the data.

claim: The CDI values were highly similar in V3A (mean CDI = 0.38 ± 5.6 × 10–3 SEM, N = 172) and CIP (mean CDI = 0.38 ± 5.7 × 10–3 SEM, N = 201) and not significantly different.
source: The CDI values were highly similar in V3A (mean CDI = 0.38 ± 5.6 × 10–3 SEM, N = 172) and CIP (mean CDI = 0.38 ± 5.7 × 10–3 SEM, N = 201) and not significantly different (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.20).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The noise correlations were almost identical in V3A (mean r = 0.17 ± 0.01 SEM, N = 404 pairs) and CIP (mean r = 0.17 ± 0.01, N = 244 pairs), and not significantly different.
source: The noise correlations were almost identical in V3A (across animals: mean r = 0.17 ± 0.01 SEM, N = 404 pairs; Monkey L: 0.15 ± 0.01, N = 206; Monkey F: 0.15 ± 0.03, N = 121; Monkey W: 0.25 ± 0.03, N = 77) and CIP (across animals: 0.17 ± 0.01, N = 244 pairs; Monkey L: 0.14 ± 0.02, N = 107; Monkey F: 0.19 ± 0.02, N = 137), and not significantly different (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, across animals: p=0.62; Monkey L: p=0.58; Monkey F: p=0.49; Figure 6B, right marginal histogram).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The signal correlations were similar in V3A (mean r = 0.40 ± 0.02 SEM) and CIP (mean r = 0.36 ± 0.03), and not significantly different.
source: We therefore quantified the signal correlations for the same pairs of neurons and found that they were also similar in V3A (across animals: mean r = 0.40 ± 0.02 SEM; Monkey L: 0.32 ± 0.03; Monkey F: 0.41 ± 0.04; Monkey W: 0.61 ± 0.04) and CIP (across animals: 0.36 ± 0.03; Monkey L: 0.26 ± 0.04; Monkey F: 0.43 ± 0.03), and not significantly different (across animals: p=0.15; Monkey L: p=0.32; Monkey F: p=0.86; Figure 6B, top marginal histogram).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The linear relationship between noise and signal correlation was not significantly different between V3A and CIP.
source: Importantly, the linear relationship between noise and signal correlation was not significantly different between the areas (ANCOVA, across animals: p=0.37; Monkey L: p=0.06; Monkey F: p=0.30).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Differences in the structure of correlated variability either within or across areas did not account for the presence of choice-related activity.
source: These results suggest that differences in the structure of correlated variability either within or across areas did not account for the presence of choice-related activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation analyses.

claim: In both V3A and CIP, the median circular difference between tilt and choice preferences was not significantly different from 0°, indicating that the tilt and choice preferences tended to align.
source: In both areas, the median circular difference between the preferences (V3A: 1.57°, N = 168; CIP: –0.75°, N = 194) was not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, both p≥0.49), indicating that the tilt and choice preferences tended to align (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: The strength of the association between tilt and choice preferences was similar in V3A and CIP.
source: To assess if the relationship between tilt and choice preferences differed between the areas, we compared the widths of the two distributions and found that they had similar circular variance (CV) values (V3A: CV = 0.34; CIP: CV = 0.33), which were not significantly different (two-sample concentration difference test, p=0.88) (Fisher, 1995). Thus, the strength of the association between tilt and choice preferences was similar in V3A and CIP.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: V3A neurons with choice-related activity had a mean tolerance of 0.65 ± 1.3 × 10–2 SEM (N = 172), whereas those without choice-related activity had a mean tolerance of 0.54 ± 7.2 × 10–3 SEM (N = 520), and the difference was significant.
source: Indeed, V3A neurons with choice-related activity had a mean tolerance of 0.65 ± 1.3 × 10–2 SEM (N = 172), whereas those without choice-related activity had a mean tolerance of 0.54 ± 7.2 × 10–3 SEM (N = 520), and the difference was significant (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test, p=3.8 × 10–9).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Choice-related activity was preferentially carried by V3A neurons with more robust 3D pose tuning, as in CIP.
source: Thus, choice-related activity was preferentially carried by V3A neurons with more robust 3D pose tuning, as in CIP.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the tolerance analysis for neurons with and without choice-related activity.

claim: Tolerance values were greater in CIP than V3A both for neurons with and without choice-related activity.
source: First, tolerance values were greater in CIP than V3A both for neurons with (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test, p=1.7 × 10–7) and without (p=1.6 × 10–4) choice-related activity (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: 3D pose tuning was more robust in CIP than V3A, regardless of whether the neurons carried choice-related activity.
source: Thus, 3D pose tuning was more robust in CIP than V3A, regardless of whether the neurons carried choice-related activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the tolerance and angular deviation analyses conditioned on choice-related activity.

claim: V3A contains extraretinal signals associated with creating stable, allocentric representations of the world.
source: Previous studies reported that V3A contains extraretinal signals associated with creating stable, allocentric representations of the world (Galletti and Battaglini, 1989; Galletti et al., 1990; Sauvan and Peterhans, 1999; Nakamura and Colby, 2002), as well as postsaccadic activity (Nakamura and Colby, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CIP possesses saccade-related activity that predicted the direction and timing of eye movements.
source: Recently, we discovered saccade-related activity in CIP that predicted the direction and timing of eye movements (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Saccade-related activity started in V3A 108 ms prior to saccade initiation.
source: Intriguingly, saccade-related activity started in V3A (a classically defined 'intermediate' visual area) 108 ms prior to saccade initiation, which was earlier than in CIP (102 ms; see Figure 8B in Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of population time courses.

claim: Saccade-related activity started in CIP 102 ms prior to saccade initiation.
source: Intriguingly, saccade-related activity started in V3A (a classically defined 'intermediate' visual area) 108 ms prior to saccade initiation, which was earlier than in CIP (102 ms; see Figure 8B in Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: The time course of saccade-related activity in V3A was distinct from the visually evoked response measured during receptive field mapping, consistent with presaccadic activity.
source: In both areas, the time course of saccade-related activity was distinct from the visually evoked response measured during receptive field mapping, consistent with presaccadic activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; see 'Discussion').
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: On trials that the saccade latency was shorter, saccade-related activity in V3A started closer to the saccade initiation.
source: On trials that the saccade latency was shorter, saccade-related activity started closer to the saccade initiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of saccade-related activity conditioned on saccade latency.

claim: The growth rate from the start of saccade-related activity to when the four curves approximately coalesced was highly correlated and inversely related to the mean saccade latency in V3A (r = –0.98, p=1.9 × 10–2).
source: Indeed, the growth rate (linear slope) from the start of saccade-related activity (ANOVA, p<0.05) to when the four curves approximately coalesced (59 ms before saccade initiation; 'Materials and methods') was highly correlated and inversely related to the mean saccade latency (r = –0.98, p=1.9 × 10–2; Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 8E.

claim: V3A activity predicts the direction and timing of upcoming saccadic eye movements.
source: Intriguingly, these results indicate that V3A activity predicts the direction and timing of upcoming saccadic eye movements.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the saccade-related activity analyses.

claim: The integrated V3A output aligned well with the CIP activity for each saccade latency quartile, as might be expected if CIP accumulates evidence from V3A in favor of particular oculomotor responses.
source: Notably, the integrated V3A output (Figure 8F, dashed curves) aligned well with the CIP activity (solid curves) for each quartile, as might be expected if CIP accumulates evidence from V3A in favor of particular oculomotor responses.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on the temporal integration analysis.

claim: V3A is not simply a 'visual area' and may suggest that there are parallel visual and saccade-related V3A-to-CIP hierarchies.
source: These results imply that V3A is not simply a 'visual area' and may suggest that there are parallel visual and saccade-related V3A-to-CIP hierarchies.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on the saccade-related activity findings.

claim: 415 (60%) of the V3A neurons had significant saccade direction tuning.
source: Across animals, 415 (60%) of the V3A neurons had significant saccade direction tuning (Monkey L: 172, 55%; Monkey F: 154, 58%; Monkey W: 89, 75%), similar to that observed in CIP (across animals: 274, 63%; Monkey L: 153, 70%; Monkey F: 121, 55%) (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the data.

claim: 274 (63%) of the CIP neurons had significant saccade direction tuning.
source: Across animals, 415 (60%) of the V3A neurons had significant saccade direction tuning (Monkey L: 172, 55%; Monkey F: 154, 58%; Monkey W: 89, 75%), similar to that observed in CIP (across animals: 274, 63%; Monkey L: 153, 70%; Monkey F: 121, 55%) (Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Saccade direction was more discriminable based on V3A (mean SDI = 0.49 ± 6.2 × 10–3 SEM, N = 415) than CIP (mean SDI = 0.41 ± 6.2 × 10–3, N = 274) responses, and the difference was statistically significant.
source: Surprisingly, saccade direction was more discriminable based on V3A (across animals: mean SDI = 0.49 ± 6.2 × 10–3 SEM, N = 415; Monkey L: 0.48 ± 0.02, N = 172; Monkey F: 0.51 ± 9.3 × 10–3, N = 154; Monkey W: 0.48 ± 0.01, N = 89) than CIP (across animals: 0.41 ± 6.2 × 10–3, N = 274; Monkey L: 0.40 ± 8.7 × 10–3, N = 153; Monkey F: 0.42 ± 8.7 × 10–3, N = 121) responses, and the difference was statistically significant (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, across animals: p=4.8 × 10–17; Monkey L: p=5.1 × 10–8; Monkey F: p=2.6 × 10–11).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: 124 V3A neurons (18%) had both choice- and saccade-related activity.
source: Across the V3A population, 124 neurons (18%) had both choice- and saccade-related activity.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the data.

claim: For V3A neurons with both choice- and saccade-related activity, choice and saccade preferences generally aligned.
source: For this subpopulation, choice and saccade preferences generally aligned (Figure 9E). The median circular difference (–1.7°) between the preferences was not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, p=0.65).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 9E.

claim: Some V3A neurons carried choice- (48, 7%) or saccade-related (291, 42%) activity only, indicating that the properties were not mutually inclusive.
source: Second, some neurons carried choice- (48, 7%) or saccade-related (291, 42%) activity only, indicating that the properties were not mutually inclusive.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of the data and inference about mutual exclusivity.

claim: Choice-related activity was associated with more robust 3D tuning in V3A, whereas saccade-related activity was associated with less robust 3D tuning.
source: Third, choice-related activity was associated with more robust 3D tuning, whereas saccade-related activity was associated with less robust 3D tuning (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that choice and saccade signals had opposite functional relationships with 3D selectivity in V3A.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The choice- and saccade-related activities were functionally distinct in V3A.
source: These results together suggest that the choice- and saccade-related activities were functionally distinct.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence about choice and saccade signals.

claim: Neurons in CIP form associations between their surface orientation and choice/saccade direction preferences such that the alignment of the tuning curves reflects whether the monkey was trained to report the near or far side of the plane.
source: Neurons in CIP form associations between their surface orientation and choice/saccade direction preferences such that the alignment of the tuning curves reflects whether the monkey was trained to report the near or far side of the plane (Elmore et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elmore et al., 2019 and Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: For V3A neurons without choice-related activity, there was no discernible association between the tilt and saccade direction preferences.
source: For neurons without choice-related activity, there was no discernible association between the tilt and saccade direction preferences since the distribution was not significantly different from uniform (Rayleigh test, p=0.08, N = 270).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: For V3A neurons with choice-related activity, the distribution of preference differences was significantly different from uniform, revealing a sensorimotor association.
source: However, for neurons with choice-related activity, the distribution was significantly different from uniform (p=1.2 × 10–18, N = 122) and the median circular difference (–1.6°) was not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, p=0.42), revealing a sensorimotor association.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: A sensorimotor association was only evident for V3A neurons with choice-related activity.
source: Thus, a sensorimotor association was only evident for V3A neurons with choice-related activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of neurons with and without choice-related activity.

claim: In CIP, sensorimotor associations were evident regardless of whether the neurons carried choice signals.
source: When we repeated this analysis for CIP, we found a striking difference from V3A (Figure 9F, right). Specifically, sensorimotor associations were evident regardless of whether the neurons carried choice signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9F.

claim: Choice signals were not necessary for sensorimotor associations in CIP, but the distribution was significantly narrower for neurons with than without choice-related activity.
source: This reveals that choice signals were not necessary for sensorimotor associations in CIP, but the distribution was significantly narrower for neurons with (CV = 0.34) than without (CV = 0.73) choice-related activity (two-sample concentration difference test, p=2.6 × 10–5; Figure 9G), indicating that sensorimotor associations were strongest for neurons with choice-related activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 9G.

claim: The distribution of preference differences was significantly broader in V3A (CV = 0.77) than CIP (CV = 0.53), indicating that sensorimotor associations were strongest in CIP.
source: We further assessed the cross-area difference in the overall strength of sensorimotor associations by comparing the widths of the V3A and CIP preference difference distributions (including neurons with and without choice-related activity). The distribution was significantly broader in V3A (CV = 0.77) than CIP (CV = 0.53; p=1.2 × 10–3), indicating that sensorimotor associations were strongest in CIP (Figure 9G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 9G.

claim: Choice-related activity statistically moderated the relationship between the robustness of 3D pose tuning and the strength of sensorimotor associations.
source: To test this, we ran a linear regression model where the absolute angular difference between the principal tilt and saccade direction preference depended on tolerance, choice-related activity, and their interaction. Both areas showed a significant interaction (both p≤1.6 × 10–3) such that tolerance had a negligible impact on the strength of the sensorimotor association for neurons without choice-related activity (V3A: slope = 0.16; CIP: slope = –0.15) but a strong impact for neurons with choice-related activity (V3A: slope = –2.2; CIP: slope = –2.5). Thus, this analysis revealed an intricate relationship between sensory, choice, and saccade-related activity in which choice signals moderated the relationship between the robustness of 3D tuning and sensorimotor associations.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing interaction effects.

claim: The findings challenge classical notions of sensorimotor dichotomies by revealing that V3A possesses saccade-related activity and defining properties of association cortex.
source: Our findings challenge classical notions of sensorimotor dichotomies by revealing that V3A possesses saccade-related activity and defining properties of association cortex, and further implicate choice-related activity as a novel factor in moderating sensorimotor processing.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: The findings implicate choice-related activity as a novel factor in moderating sensorimotor processing.
source: Our findings challenge classical notions of sensorimotor dichotomies by revealing that V3A possesses saccade-related activity and defining properties of association cortex, and further implicate choice-related activity as a novel factor in moderating sensorimotor processing.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the moderation analysis.

claim: The finding that the time course of saccade-related activity in CIP closely resembled the temporally integrated V3A output may suggest that some presaccadic signals originate in a region of visual cortex whose feedforward input includes V1 and V2.
source: The finding that the time course of saccade-related activity in CIP closely resembled the temporally integrated V3A output may further suggest that some presaccadic signals originate in a region of visual cortex whose feedforward input includes V1 and V2 (Zeki, 1980; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991), thus challenging classical notions of sensorimotor dichotomies.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The current findings are consistent with CIP accumulating evidence provided by V3A in favor of particular oculomotor responses, which raises the possibility that some of the integration-like properties of LIP may reflect bottom-up input.
source: This finding is also consistent with CIP accumulating evidence provided by V3A in favor of particular oculomotor responses, which raises the possibility that some of the integration-like properties of LIP (Shadlen and Newsome, 1996; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002) may reflect bottom-up input (Lewis and Van Essen, 2000; Premereur et al., 2015; Van Dromme et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivating CIP might impair saccadic responses during decision-making tasks.
source: In that case, inactivating CIP, which is architectonically distinct from LIP (Katsuyama et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2020), might impair saccadic responses during decision-making tasks.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Reversible inactivation of CIP during a depth structure categorization task was found to delay saccadic responses.
source: Consistent with this, reversible inactivation of CIP during a depth structure categorization task was found to delay saccadic responses (Van Dromme et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Van Dromme et al., 2016.

claim: The saccade-related activity cannot be explained by visual responses alone.
source: Nevertheless, several lines of evidence suggest that the observed saccade-related activity cannot be explained by visual responses alone.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: A presaccadic signal may begin in V3A 7 ms before CIP.
source: Examination of the time courses provided some evidence that a presaccadic signal may begin in V3A 7 ms before CIP, consistent with the possibility of a V3A-to-CIP oculomotor hierarchy.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on examination of time courses.

claim: The current findings suggest that V3A and CIP may contain presaccadic signals, but a thorough evaluation of this possibility will require future studies.
source: The current findings therefore suggest that V3A and CIP may contain presaccadic signals, but a thorough evaluation of this possibility will require future studies.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the speculative nature of the presaccadic signal interpretation and calls for future work.

claim: Finding sensorimotor associations in V3A implies that sensorimotor processing traditionally linked to parietal cortex already occurs in an 'intermediate visual area,' suggesting that V3A may be more appropriately classified as an early association region.
source: Many V3A neurons showed functional associations between their orientation, choice, and saccade direction preferences, as in CIP (Elmore et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020b). Finding these associations in V3A implies that sensorimotor processing traditionally linked to parietal cortex already occurs in an 'intermediate visual area,' suggesting that V3A may be more appropriately classified as an early association region.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the sensorimotor association findings.

claim: The cross-area differences in saccade direction discrimination and sensorimotor associations may reflect a transition from lower-level representations of saccade-related signals to higher-level sensorimotor associations.
source: Intriguingly, saccade direction discrimination was greater in V3A (where saccade-related activity was associated with poorer 3D pose tuning) while sensorimotor associations were stronger in CIP (where no relationship between saccade-related activity and the robustness of 3D tuning was evident). These cross-area differences may reflect a transition from lower-level representations of saccade-related signals to higher-level sensorimotor associations and parallel the observed changes in visual feature selectivity.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on the cross-area comparisons.

claim: The large V3A sample revealed a heterogeneous population in which neurons ranged from representing low-level visual features to high-level object properties.
source: Our large V3A sample revealed a heterogeneous population in which neurons ranged from representing low-level visual features to high-level object properties.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the tolerance and tuning analyses.

claim: Earlier discrepancies in V3A findings may reflect a combination of heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and the possibility of functionally distinct modules within V3A.
source: Earlier discrepancies may reflect a combination of this heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and the possibility of functionally distinct modules within V3A.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference about why previous studies reached different conclusions.

claim: Variability in how V3A was defined may have contributed to discrepancies in previous findings.
source: Another factor that may have contributed to the discrepancies is variability in how V3A was defined (Nakhla et al., 2021), highlighting the continued importance of using functional and anatomical localization methods in future investigations of this relatively understudied area.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference supported by citation to Nakhla et al., 2021.

claim: Some V3A neurons were selective for gradients of relative disparity.
source: For some V3A neurons, we found that orientation tuning curve shape (but not gain) was highly tolerant to distance, implying 3D pose tuning. Because the perspective cues in our stimuli were independent of distance, the gain changes must have been driven by stereoscopic cues. This implies that these neurons were selective for gradients of relative disparity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the tolerance analysis and stimulus design.

claim: Some V3A neurons may have been selective for absolute disparity gradients, similar to some middle temporal (MT) area neurons.
source: Other V3A neurons showed orientation tuning at a single distance. These neurons may have been selective for absolute disparity gradients, similar to some middle temporal (MT) area neurons (Nguyenkim and DeAngelis, 2003).
evidence: The claim is speculative inference supported by citation to Nguyenkim and DeAngelis, 2003.

claim: Selectivity for absolute disparity gradients may account for suppressive effects previously reported within the classical receptive fields of V3A neurons.
source: Selectivity for absolute disparity gradients may further account for suppressive effects previously reported within the classical receptive fields of V3A neurons (Gaska et al., 1987) since the stimuli were presented at screen distance only and therefore would stimulate portions of the receptive field with non-preferred disparities.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference connecting the current findings to previous observations.

claim: One possibility is that absolute disparity representations (in V1) are used to construct absolute disparity gradient detectors (in V3A, MT) and then pose selectivity (in V3A, PIP, CIP).
source: One possibility is that absolute disparity representations (in V1) are used to construct absolute disparity gradient detectors (in V3A, MT) and then pose selectivity (in V3A, PIP, CIP).
evidence: The claim is speculative inference about the hierarchical construction of 3D representations.

claim: Contemporary interpretations of choice signals include a mix of feedforward contributions to decision processes, the structure of correlated variability, attention, cognitive and behavioral factors, as well as feedback.
source: Contemporary interpretations of choice signals include a mix of feedforward contributions to decision processes, the structure of correlated variability, attention, cognitive and behavioral factors, as well as feedback (Celebrini and Newsome, 1994; Britten et al., 1996; Dodd et al., 2001; Haefner et al., 2013; Gu et al., 2014; Ruff and Cohen, 2014; Smolyanskaya et al., 2015; Cumming and Nienborg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The current findings are consistent with a feedforward cascade and build-up of choice signals, which may reflect greater contributions of CIP than V3A to 3D perceptual decisions.
source: Despite these complexities, the current findings are consistent with a feedforward cascade and build-up of choice signals, which may reflect greater contributions of CIP than V3A to 3D perceptual decisions.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on the temporal and prevalence patterns of choice signals.

claim: Neurons that carry choice signals tend to have resolved sensory ambiguities about the information being discriminated, allowing them to more directly contribute to decisions.
source: This is consistent with reports that neurons that carry choice signals tend to have resolved sensory ambiguities about the information being discriminated, allowing them to more directly contribute to decisions (Liu et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013 and Chang et al., 2020b.

claim: Choice signals may be confounded with feature-based attentional modulation, but this is unlikely to explain the current findings.
source: Although choice signals may be confounded with feature-based attentional modulation (Cohen and Newsome, 2008), this is unlikely to explain our findings.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the nature of the observed effects and citation to Cohen and Newsome, 2008.

claim: Attention is largely associated with changes in response magnitude.
source: Attention is largely associated with changes in response magnitude (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reynolds and Heeger, 2009.

claim: The findings reveal a multifaceted landscape of functional associations between sensory, choice-, and motor-related activity.
source: These findings thus reveal a multifaceted landscape of functional associations between sensory, choice-, and motor-related activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the overall pattern of results.

claim: The findings imply a novel role for choice signals in sensorimotor processing that might reflect the temporal cascade of sensory processing, response selection, and motor action.
source: They further imply a novel role for choice signals in sensorimotor processing that might reflect the temporal cascade of sensory processing, response selection, and motor action.
evidence: The claim is speculative inference based on the moderation analysis and temporal patterns.

claim: All procedures followed the National Institutes of Health's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (Protocol G005229).
source: All procedures followed the National Institutes of Health's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (Protocol G005229).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Three male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta; Monkey L: 6 years of age; Monkey F: 5 years; Monkey W: 5 years) were used in the study.
source: Three male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta; Monkey L: 6 years of age; Monkey F: 5 years; Monkey W: 5 years) were surgically implanted with a Delrin ring for head restraint and a removable recording grid for guiding electrodes.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the subjects.

claim: Planar surfaces subtending 20° of visual angle were presented at the center of the screen.
source: Briefly, planar surfaces subtending 20° of visual angle were presented at the center of the screen.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the stimulus properties.

claim: The stimuli were defined by 250 nonoverlapping dots that were uniformly distributed across the plane and rendered with stereoscopic and perspective cues.
source: They were defined by 250 nonoverlapping dots that were uniformly distributed across the plane and rendered with stereoscopic and perspective cues.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the stimulus properties.

claim: All combinations of eight tilts (0–315°, 45° steps) and four slants (15–60°, 15° steps) plus the frontoparallel plane (tilt undefined, slant = 0°) were presented (N = 33).
source: All combinations of eight tilts (0–315°, 45° steps) and four slants (15–60°, 15° steps) plus the frontoparallel plane (tilt undefined, slant = 0°) were presented (N = 33).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the stimulus conditions.

claim: All orientations were presented at four distances (37, 57, 97, and 137 cm; N = 132 unique poses).
source: All orientations were presented at four distances (37, 57, 97, and 137 cm; N = 132 unique poses).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the stimulus conditions.

claim: Keeping the fixation distance constant while varying the plane's distance ensured that the monkeys could not rely on local absolute disparity cues to judge 3D orientation.
source: Keeping its distance constant while varying the plane's distance was a key design feature (Nguyenkim and DeAngelis, 2003; Hegdé and Van Essen, 2005; Ban and Welchman, 2015; Alizadeh et al., 2018; Henderson et al., 2019) that conferred two advantages over yoking the distance of the stimulus and fixation point (Banks et al., 2001; Hillis et al., 2004). First, it ensured that the monkeys could not rely on local absolute disparity cues to judge 3D orientation (Elmore et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020a; Chang et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the experimental design.

claim: Keeping the fixation distance constant while varying the plane's distance allowed dissociation of the effects of stimulus distance and vergence signals on neuronal responses.
source: Second, it allowed us to dissociate the effects of stimulus distance and vergence signals (which would have otherwise been confounded) on the neuronal responses, which is important because V3A and CIP carry extraretinal signals.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental design and known properties of the areas.
